content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: Authors present a method that takes a set of multi-view RGB+depth images of a single scene as input, and trains a generator that can synthesise many scenes with similar characteristics to the original, incorporating variations at different scales – e.g. novel compositions of similar (but non-identical) objects. The proposed approach represents the generated scenes as a NeRF conditioned on a multi-scale voxel grid. It is trained with (patchwise) 2D discrimination on images taken from random viewpoints, similar to SinGAN (but now the generations are renderings). The method is evaluated on eight synthetic scenes and fewer real scenes, with reasonable results on the synthetic ones, exceeding the performance of baseline designed for larger (multi-scene) datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- The proposed model is novel (to the best of my knowledge), and clearly described.

- The empirical evaluations shows that the proposed method significantly out-performs the chosen baselines on the particular task – successfully avoiding the strong mode-collapse that occurs when methods designed for large datasets are applied to a single scene
there are ablation experiments present, that justify various design decisions within the model.

- Top-level claims are generation of general scenes, but experiments focus on simple, highly-regular synthetic scenes. On the two real scenes included (in the appendix), the results are unimpressive. The claims early in the paper are therefore too strong, and should be weakened (or the method demonstrated to work better on more general scenes).

- There is no comparison to a baseline that first reconstructs a voxelised representation of the scene (e.g. using standard NeRF), then builds a 3D GAN directly from this. This is notable particularly given the proposed method already has a loss requiring it to reconstruct the inputs.

- Generated scenes are only visualised from a small range of viewpoints (high elevation). This makes the task of generating geometry that reprojects reasonably (i.e. looks plausible) much easier. There is no evidence that the scenes have realistic 3D structure; this could be resolved by visualising much more diverse viewpoints – e.g. fly-throughs, or at very least shallower elevation angles for the 'turntable' renderings. Including depth-maps alongside the renderings would also help.

- The discussion of related work is missing mention of 2D generative models trained from single images – most notably SinGAN [Shaham, ICCV '19]. SinGAN is cited (in the introduction and method), but these works seem sufficient close in spirit that they justify their own paragraph in the related work section.

- The proposed representation seems to require that scenes occupy a bounded volume (e.g. unit cube), and beyond this scale, there is nothing to prevent the model simply repeating the content. This somewhat restricts the scope of scenes to which it is applicable. In particular, it is not possible to handle distant objects even at lower fidelity (as in representations such as MIP-NeRF 360).

- According to the appendix, several architectural hyperparameters of the model require setting differently for different scenes
the use of a 2D convolution at the finest scale is not shown in fig. 2. This also means (c.f. GIRAFFE and similar methods) that there is no guarantee the finer details are 3D-consistent when seen from different viewpoints. However, this is not discussed nor evaluated. An approach such as the 'dual discriminator' of EG3D would mitigate this.

- Why is the main task (generating 'variations' given a scene for which multi-view RGB+D images are available, but without explicitly reconstructing it) actually useful in practice? It seems that all applications (editing etc.) could be achieved more directly via other means, by first reconstructing the initial scene explicitly. Note that the proposed method already requires MVS to have been run on the input images (for the depth supervision), and then also finds latents that reconstruct the particular scene, so the 3D reconstruction problem is essentially solved already.

- Object-level editing ('recomposition') in particular (fig. 1) is more natural with a more-explicitly object-centric representation, rather than relying on CNN feature maps approximately-aligning with object boundaries. There is plenty of literature in this area, which should at least be discussed briefly, e.g. BlobGAN (Epstein, ECCV '22), O3V (Henderson, NeurIPS '20), and uORF (Yu, ICLR '22).

- Suggestion: the natural scenes shown in the appendix are not ideal to show off the benefits of the model. They both contain a single 'focal' object, meaning that it is challenging to even define what spatially-compositional variations should look like. I think that with (e.g.) many, varied mountains in the scene, or other quasi-repetitive structures (as in the synthetic datasets), the shift between synthetic and real data would be less, and perhaps performance on such real scenes would be better.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- the writing is clear, fluent and pleasant-to-read throughout
- the description of the method is generally clear and straightforward to follow, though precisely how the final 2D stage is incorporated is not entirely clear
- the presented architecture is novel (to the best of my knowledge); however it is a fairly straightforward composition of existing parts (Xu '21; NeRF; WGAN-GP; etc.), without any critical technical contribution
- the description appears sufficiently detailed to reimplement the method; however as always there are likely precise technical choices necessary to reproduce the exact results, hence the authors are encouraged to make the code public following acceptance, to ensure reproducibility
- the ablation SinGRAV-MLP is not adequately described
- there is insufficient discussion of how the editing operations (fig. 1) are performed
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I enjoyed reading the paper. The proposed model is motivated and described clearly. Experiments seem to have been conducted carefully, with sufficient analysis of ablations present to justify design decisions. However, the empirical results are insufficient to justify the claims (see above) – particularly on real scenes. Demonstrating the method mainly on synthetic data creates a very 'circular' setup where a 3D scene is manually created, then rendered, then represented in the latent space of the proposed method, then edited. Clearly this is an unrealistic and suboptimal pipeline, and convincing performance on real-world scenes is necessary to persuade me that the method is practically useful.

content.title: Response1 to Reviewer Uy5C
content.comment:
**Revise the claim at the beginning of the paper**

Since the range of scene types that beyond single object is really huge, it is difficult to some extent to precisely define the range of scenes where SinGRAV can work well.  Thus we try our best to collect data covering different types of scenes, which demonstrate a considerable diversity on geometry, textures and arrangement, instead of only exhibiting circular or quasi-repetitive patterns,  to investigate the performance of the proposed framework. At the same time, we also provide two real-world scenes with a large scale and fine textures to test the framework, on which SinGRAV roughly works but fails to model the fine textures due to the limitation brought by the voxel-based representation and the memory consumption triggered during the training. We are openminded to revise the description of the claim at the beginning of our paper to make it less strong. And further suggestions on this from you are welcomed.


**Comparison to a baseline of first-reconstruct-then-train**

For the designing of our framework, we propose to use a combination of spatial inductive bias and joint discrimination on the rendered depth-the byproduct of the volume rendering. This design enables us to resolve the implausible spatial arrangement issue without introducing much extra computation/memory cost, since the discriminator keeps working in the 2D domain. *However, when considering directly letting the discriminator operate in a 3D domain, this necessitates a discriminator with 3D convolutions, which will significantly increase the memory and computation cost of training, which consequently limits the maximum volume resolution that can be adopted.*


**Requirement of modeling a bounded scene**

Actually, for a 3D scene model we are focusing on, the borders between the foreground and the background of the scene are dynamically changed, which is totally different from a reconstruction model, in which only a single scene is considered and the borders will not change. Modeling background in a scene generation model will trigger a challenge: how we can efficiently represent and generate the background for a new scene with good continuities on the borders between foreground and background.  Since you are familiar with this area and have known about a great number of the related works in this domain, you may notice that the generative models for object-centric scenes separately model the background. But we need to note that those models don't need to carefully consider the continuity between the foreground object and the background modeled by another MLP. How to support seamless and efficient (for memory) generation of foreground and background is a really worthwhile problem to study.


**3D structure of the generated scene**

In the leftmost of  Figure 7 of the manuscript, we show an example of the point cloud extracted from the rgb-d rendering of a generated scene from SinGRAV, which reveals the underlying 3D structure for the scene  to extent.

Besides, since we want to model some background in our model and some scenes with no explicit background-foreground separation, e.g., the grass and flowers,  we choose to supervise the views from higher views to avoid letting the rays shoot into an infinitely distant area that is not modeled by the current framework.  As discussed above, modeling background within a scene generation model and maintaining the continuity between the foreground and the background is not trivial and worthwhile to be studied in a future work.


**View consistency** 

In the conclusion part of the manuscript, we mentioned that the 2D renderer will inevitably introduce the view inconsistency issue.  And thanks for your suggestion on incorporating the dual discrimination proposed in EG3D to resolve this issue. *We now have already taken this dual discrimination in our pipeline*,  as described in the paragraph "Adversarial loss" in page 5 of the manuscript.


**Object-level editing**

We agree that object-level editing is more natural when the scene is well segmented and each object is separately represented in some forms. However, automatic disentanglement of different instances within a single scene (what our framework is working on) is not always that easy.  In the scope of our paper, we are focusing on the editing that is supported by the multi-scale scene representation learned by our model SinGRAV, which enables us to naively modify the radiance volume of a coarser level and the generators will automatically harmonize the modifications. Besides, our model is also designed to generate different variants of the input scene automatically. 

We now provide the detailed descriptions of the application operations in Section A.1.4 of the supplementary material. Please refer to that section for  more details.



**Capturing more suitable real scenes for demonstrations**

Thanks for your suggestion and please see General Response.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This submission proposes and approach to learn a generative model from a single 3D scene. The proposed method allows to generate plausible and diverse variations from a single scene. The proposed approach is evaluated in several single-scene datasets obtaining compelling results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
 - The problem of learning generative models for 3D scenes is a hot-topic and this paper introduces some interesting observations.
  - The technical approach is technically correct and the applications spanning editing, composition, and animation are interesting.

  Weaknesses:
 - The main weakness of this submission is conceptual. One may argue what is the value of learning a generative model for a single scene, as opposed to just learning to reconstruction the input views (eg. NeRF style)? From the reviewers perspective, the applications shown in this paper are orthogonal from the fact that the model is generative (eg. One can tackle editing, composition and animation without a generative model). I believe what this model is actually doing is overfitting a GAN to a given scene, which is not necessarily the goal of other generative models like GRAF or pi-gan. 
 - In addition, it seems hard to evaluate the value of the contributions without seeing empirical results on real-world data as opposed to synthetic scenes.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: - The paper is clear and easy to understand. The main implementation details are outlines in the main manuscript
content.summary_of_the_review: This submission introduces a 3D generative model for a single scene. The proposed is technically correct but has a major conceptual flaw (see weaknesses). I would be willing to change my score if the authors can argue the value of overfitting a generative model to a single scene.

content.title: Response to Reviewer RnBn
content.comment:
1. **The value of training a generative model on a single scene**

   

   Firstly, training a generative model on a single scene enables us to generate more variants, which is useful to enrich the 3D content demonstrated in the future immersive applications or provide some inspirations to the designers by the randomness of the generated scenes.

   

   Secondly, for the application tasks, the value of training a generative is described below:

   ​	(a) For scene composition, training a generative model can produce more diversity quickly and automatically without manually copying and adjusting each instances, during which people need to elaborately think about how to edit each instance to make the scene more interesting and diverse.

   ​	(b) For scene animation, training a generative model can not only support for animating the original scene by reconstructing it, but also support to animate the generated scenes, which substantially add more possibilities. *Besides, importantly, training a generative model on a single scene produces a series of multi-scale radiance volumes and corresponding generators for supporting automatic animation. The animation is achieved by simply injecting random noise in the volume of several levels and letting the generators harmonize the animation*. *Instead, without training a generative model, there is not such a meaningful multi-scale volume space and generators, people need to animate the reconstructed scene manually, which is really cumbersome*

   ​	(c) For scene editing, training a generative model not only supports to edit the original scene but also the generated ones. Particularly, training a generative model produces a tool to ease the editing, that is, the editing can be done by simply modifying the radiance volume at a coarser level in our model without the need to manually harmonize the edited scenes (e.g., the discontinuities produced by the naive removing and moving operations.)

   Additionally, we provide the implementation details of these applications in Section A.1.4 of the supplementary material, which would be helpful for fully understanding the application value we mentioned above.


2. **Results on the real-world scenes**

   Please see our response in General Response.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Jheg
content.comment:
1. **Discussions on the challenges encountered in 3D**

   Thanks for your constructive suggestion. Please see the General Response, where we explained more about the challenges when the idea of learning internal distributions is extended to 3D scene generation. We will incorporate more discussions in the revised version of the manuscript.

2. **Discussions on the limitations of scene types**

   As discussed in SinGAN, it will fail when the global structure is highly important for the entire scene, for example, when the scene dominantly contain a single object with high semantic structures such as a human face or a car.  Naturally, our framework will also fail when a 3D scene has such characteristics.

   Besides, considering the 3D scene generation task we are focusing on, for which the representation capacity is a common issue. Regarding the voxel-based representation and the memory/computation consumption in the training process,  SinGRAV is not able to model a large scene with fine textures, as illustrated in the real-world examples we showed in the supplementary materials.

   We will incorporate more discussions on the limitations in the revised version.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a 3D generative model for general natural scenes, using only 2 training views. The authors propose to use a tri-plane as the neural radiance field and apply GAN loss on pyramid stages. The key insight is that a natural scene often contains multiple constituents whose geometry, texture, and spatial arrangements follow some clear patterns, but still exhibit rich variations over different regions within the same scene. The authors demonstrate the ability of SinGRAV in generating plausible and diverse variations from a single scene, the merits of SinGRAV over state-of-the-art generative neural scene methods, as well as the versatility of SinGRAV by its use in a variety of applications, spanning 3D scene editing, composition, and animation. The corresponding codebase will be provided accordingly.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- This paper proposes to use only two views to render the novel view of 360 degrees. Although it is only limited to specific scenes (e.g. containing homogeneous patterns), the visual results look good.
- The motivation of capturing and reusing homogeneous feature looks interesting.

Weaknesses:
- A very important reference [1] is missing, and that is my biggest concern. Many designed components in this work are already proposed in [1]. For example, the GAN loss, depth-supervision, and adopting radiance field as the main backbone. Meanwhile, the `Progressive Strided Ray Sampling` in [1] is also similar to the proposed pyramid training strategy, where both of them are calculating loss on multi-scale resolution, as suggested by the SinGAN [3]. My final rating will highly depend on whether the authors can clearly address the differences between these two works.
- How are the camera pose of training views obtained? This is an important question because in practice it is hard to estimate the camera poses using only 2 views, either using SfM or Slam. The vanilla NeRF takes 100 training views to get a roughly correct camera pose using colmap [2], and SinNeRF [1] does not require a camera pose since it only needs a single training view. In real scenarios, even if you can train a 3D GAN using only two views, it is hard to get the camera pose of these two views before training starts.
- In figure 4, the randomly generated view seems to be not view-consistent. I guess those are from the one view of different random seeds? I think the caption should be more accurate in case of any misunderstanding.
- In figure 5, the author mentioned "All baselines encounter severe mode-collapse issues". What are the visual results of the proposed method? It should be included here for a fair comparison.

References:
[1] SinNeRF: Training Neural Radiance Fields on Complex Scenes from a Single Image.
[2] Structure-from-Motion Revisited.
[3] Learning a Generative Model from a Single Natural Image.

content.title: Response to Reviewer hgiA
content.comment:
1. **Discussion between SinGRAV and SinNeRF [1]**:

    Our framework SinGRAV is different from SinNeRF [1] from the following aspects:

   (a) From the task aspect,  our framework aims at training a *generative model* enabling 		**generating different variants** resembling the original scene while SinNeRF is proposed to **reconstruct** a neural radiance field from a single view of the depicted scene.

   (b) In our framework, the depth supervision is designed to be a joint discrimination of the rgb and depth patches for the generated fake samples. In SinNeRF, the depth supervision is designed in the form of some kind of regularizers to force the consistency between depth of the reference view and the projected unseen view.

   (c) Our patch discrimination operates in RGB-D domain, while the patch discrimination in SinNeRF only cares the texture. Besides, we are utilizing the patch discrimination to learn the internal distributions within the training scene to support generation, while SinNeRF utilizes the patch discrimination on RGB images to increase the texture of the reconstructed scene. 

   (d) The scene representation capacity is growing in different scales in the multi-scale training of our framework while it is fixed by the NeRF backbone in SinNeRF.

   (e) Since SinGRAV is a generative model, once it is trained, it can be adopted to generate abundant different scenes while SinNeRF is not able to achieve this since it is not a generative model.

   (f) As a generative model, our framework enables a variety of application tasks by naively manipulating the radiance volumes of coarser levels and letting the generators at finer scales to harmonize the modification. 

   

2. **Discussion between SinGRAV and SinGAN [3]:**

   ​	 Please see the General Response.

   

 3. **Results in Figure 4**

    In each row, we provides three examples generated by different noise seeds. We will make the caption clearer.

    

   4. **Results in Figure 5 for fair comparison**

      We put the results of corresponding examples in Figure 4 and we didn't provide them in Figure 5 again for saving the space.

      

   5. **More about the settings of our work and data collection**

       As stated in the Paragraph-**Data** in Page 6, we used 200 views of a single scene for training. We believe that the camera poses can be easily reconstructed by COLMAP from such a number of images under different viewpoints.

       

6. **Novelty of SinGRAV**

   As generally recognized by other reviewers, we are the first one to investigate the task. Besides, we explain more on the challenges we need to tackle and the designs we choose to incorporate to cope with the challenges. Please see the General Response. Besides, we clarify more about the differences of our framework in the above discussions.

content.title: General Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their reviews and constructive suggestions.  We are happy to see that reviewers think  that our work is (1) novel [Reviewer Jheg, Uy5C] and think that (2) "the motivation of capturing and reusing homogeneous feature looks interesting" [Reviewer hgiA], (3) "The architecture is carefully designed" [Reviewer Jheg], (4) "the applications spanning editing , composition and animation are interesting"[Reviewer RnBn],  and our work (5)"obtains compelling results" and "introduces some interesting observations"  [Reviewer RnBn] .

We will first address shared comments in the General Response and then response to individual ones separately to each reviewer.


-----
### Shared comments

1. **Discussions between our framework and SinGAN** [Reviewer hgiA,  Jheg, Uy5C]

   Overall, although the idea of learning internal distributions is generally inspired by sinGAN, we observed unique challenges when it is directly extended to 3D scene generation, for which we carefully incorporate the designs in our framework. Those considerations and designs make our framework different from SinGAN. 

   

   ***Challenges:***

   (a) ***Suitable scene representation:*** For localizing the training, an appropriate neural scene representation needs to be carefully considered.

   (b) ***Implausible spatial arrangement:*** The goal of learning internal distributions within a single scene necessitates a limited   receptive field of the generators and discriminators and a multi-scale training strategy,  which jointly make it necessary to start the training at a very coarse level. **However, we observed that, the patch discrimination on the renderings with small resolutions at coarser levels can not distinguish the effects produced by the implausible geometric arrangement of the content within the generated scene**.

   **Differences:**  

   (1)  As  fully investigated in the manuscript, the goal of learning internal distributions triggers a design choice of scene representation with locality modeling in SinGRAV.

   (2) To resolve the issues of implausible geometric arrangement and avoid highly increasing the computation and memory cost, our remedy is to use a combination of (a) spatial inductive bias injected in the coarsest level and (b) the joint discrimination on depth map - a byproduct of the volume rendering  technique.

   (3) We further incorporate a 2D super-resolving module at the finest level to achieve a higher resolution of renderings to reduce the memory and computation consumption. For this, we also incorporate corresponding loss terms and the dual discrimination strategy to achieve better details and better maintain view consistency. 

   (4) The generator and discriminator operate in different domains in SinGRAV,  while they operate in the same domain (image domain) in SinGAN.

------

2. **Results on real-world data** [Reviewer RnBn, Uy5C]

   We believe that the analysis of limitations of one work is also important for facilitating the future research, **which is especially meaningful in SinGRAV as it is the first exploration on this task**. 

   The synthetic data we collected for validating our framework covers a variety of scene types, on which SinGRAV works well. This makes us believe that SinGRAV can also work on the real captured data of the scenes with similar characteristics to the synthetic data (e.g., as suggested by Reviewer Uy5C, the scenes with quasi-repetitive structures. )

   For the experimental results demonstrated in the supplementary material, as suggested by Reviewer Uy5C, those two real-world data examples are not ideal for showing off the benefits. Instead, although SinGRAV produces reasonable results,  limitations can be exhibited to some extent on those two scenes. As discussed in the manuscript, the voxel representation in the current framework limits the representation capacity of SinGRAV, which makes it not sufficient to represent the fine textures in those two examples. We believe that it is worthwhile to study more on this in the future work.
